nameStory: The word 'pea' comes from the Latin 'pisum,' which ancient Romans used for this same plant over 2,000 years ago. Interestingly, we used to call a single one a 'pease' (like 'geese' for multiple geese), but people mistakenly thought 'pease' was plural and started saying 'pea' for just one. So our modern word 'pea' actually comes from a grammar mistake that stuck around!
description: The common pea is the same climbing garden vegetable you might grow in your backyard or find at the farmer's market. This annual vine uses delicate tendrils to climb up supports, reaching 3-6 feet tall in a single growing season. The plant produces the familiar plump green pods filled with round, sweet peas that we love to eat fresh from the garden or find frozen in the grocery store.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Plump, bright green pods about 2-4 inches long that feel smooth and slightly waxy. When you gently squeeze a mature pod, you can feel the round peas inside like little marbles. The pods split open along both seams when ripe, revealing 4-8 perfectly round, sweet-tasting green peas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive compound leaves with 2-3 pairs of oval leaflets that feel smooth and slightly waxy. Each leaf ends in branching, curly tendrils that feel like thin green wire and wrap around anything they touch for support.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic pea-family flowers that look like tiny white butterflies, about 1 inch across. They have the characteristic 'sweet pea' shape with one large upper petal (the banner) and smaller side petals, appearing in clusters of 1-3 flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing vine that uses curly tendrils to grab onto fences, trellises, or other plants. The stems are hollow, smooth, and surprisingly sturdy, with a fresh 'green' smell when broken.

habitat: You'll find pea plants primarily in gardens, farms, and occasionally escaped near agricultural areas throughout New England. They prefer rich, well-drained soil and cool, moist conditions. As an escaped crop plant, they sometimes appear in disturbed areas like old garden sites or compost piles, but they rarely persist in truly wild settings.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted in early spring when soil is workable. Young plants emerge with their characteristic compound leaves and start sending out exploring tendrils.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season, with white butterfly-like flowers appearing followed quickly by developing pods. This is when you'll see the familiar green pea pods forming and filling out.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to yellow and die back as cool weather returns. Any remaining pods turn brown and papery, eventually splitting to release mature seeds.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence - this annual plant completes its entire life cycle in one growing season and dies with the first hard frost.

funFact: Pea plants actually improve the soil they grow in! Like all legumes, they have special bacterial partners living in little nodules on their roots that capture nitrogen from the air and turn it into plant food - essentially making fertilizer out of thin air.
confusionNotes: Garden peas might be confused with wild vetch species, but vetches have much smaller, more numerous leaflets and typically purple or pink flowers rather than white ones. Sweet pea flowers (Lathyrus) look very similar but are usually colorful and fragrant - remember that edible peas have plain white flowers.
contextualKnowledge: While we call them 'peas,' many other unrelated plants share this name - like sweet peas (which are toxic), black-eyed peas (actually beans), and even beach peas (a native wild relative). True garden peas are always safe to eat raw right from the pod, unlike some of their look-alikes.
compareHints: Common pea is the only Pisum species you'll encounter in New England, but it's closely related to the wild beach pea and various vetch species in the same legume family. Unlike its wild cousins, garden peas have much larger, fleshier pods and bigger individual peas inside, plus they always have white flowers rather than the purples and pinks of their relatives.
